en: The *Zichi* (Record of Aid and Support), the *Liti* (Establishment of the Title), and the *Shiyi* (Gathering of Meanings); by the Master of the Buddha-Wisdom, Daobiao of Moyuntang.

These are the six [sections]: the title of the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya), the title of the *Xingshichao* (Commentary on Ritual Practice), and the titles of the *Zhiji* (Record of Aid and Support). Part One.
The first six characters apply to the title as a whole, while the last three characters refer specifically to the commentary that explains the text.

Regarding the application of the first six characters to the title, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The 'Four Parts' (*Sifen*) is the specific name for one of the five schools and the general designation for this entire tradition.

From this, the sense of these characters applying to the present school can be seen. As for their application to the title of the *Chao* (Sub-commentary), if we consider it in relation to various other texts...
The original titles were distinct as individual designations; now, based on the ancient chapters, more than fifty schools have collectively offered their exegesis, thereby forming this general title.
These two general titles must be followed by the characters "Zizhi ji" (Record of Aiding and Sustaining) to constitute the current specific title.
This distinguishes it from records of other Vinayas or other commentaries; it is specifically the *Sifenlü xingshichao* (Commentary on the Practice and Rites of the Four-Part Vinaya).

The *Zichi ji* (Record of Support) states that, for instance, Xingzong’s interpretation of the title of the *Shu* (Commentary)—taking the general and forming the specific—is merely based on the traditional exegesis;
it only distinguishes between the "agent" and the "object" without clarifying the meaning of "taking the general. Therefore, the meaning of the two general titles is useless;

even if there were a basis for following them, it would still be vague and diffuse. The title of the *Lüti chao* (Commentary on the Title of the Vinaya) is explained below according to its own commentary.

Regarding the necessity of recording the title according to the present [tradition], there are three sections for the detailed explanation: first, an account of the original intent in establishing the title; second, an account of differing interpretations from the past;
and third, an account of the correct meaning according to the present [tradition].

Within the first section, it is necessary that the title established here accords with the fundamental tenets; furthermore, the original basis for the establishment of the title in this present *Chao* (Digest) is rooted in the *Xingshi* (Ritual Practice).

The intent of the Vinaya school deeply accords with the source of the teachings; its radiance reflects back through nine generations, providing a model for those who have received its grace. Among all religious schools, none surpasses this intent.

Expressions concerning "practical conduct" (*xing-shi*) appear throughout various texts. As the subtext states: "To manifest practical conduct in worldly affairs" and "to sharpen one's resolve for practical conduct.

Furthermore, the preface to the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) says: "The Vinaya-piṭaka is vast and essential; practical conduct is its strategic plan. Thus, it is known that "practical conduct" (*xing-shi*) refers to this.
The Tathāgata originally taught the source of transformation as the fundamental principle for exposition; it serves as the grand framework for the three practices and the pivotal core of this school.
Now, the aim of this *Jiaozhi* (Explanatory Notes) lies in the *Xingshi ji* (Record of Ritual Practice).

The text of the commentary must accord with the intent of the original notes, and the title *Jiaozhi* (Supporting and Sustaining) was established so that its meaning would not be misrepresented. Thus, one knows that *Jiaozhi* is indeed *Xingshi*. Furthermore, regarding practice...
Taking "active creation" as the name and "aiding completion" as the designation, the meaning of accomplishing the task through active creation is not remote.
Regarding the "task," there are two kinds, divided into cessation and practice. Cessation consists of abandoning what is non-virtuous to accomplish one's own conduct;

practice consists solely of cultivating goodness, wherein the multitude collectively and uniformly cultivate these two. Thus, these two accomplish the two types of observance (*samvara*). It should be known that the three modes of conduct are thus...

The second is the "Two Retentions" (Erchi). As the subsequent text states: "That which is called one division [of the Vinaya] is unified under the Three Practices (Sanxing), not exceeding the meaning of the Two Retentions.

The Preface to the *Yi-chao* says: "The arrayed multitude of the Two Retentions is unified under the Three Practices. Thus, we know that the title of the present record follows the model of the *Chao*’s title.

Its own sub-commentary explains: "Respectfully inheriting the purport of the ritual practice (*xingshi*), it is titled *Zi-chi* (Aiding Retention), so as not to deviate from the principle of the Three Practices."

Le unrolls the scroll and records here that the intent behind establishing this title is exhausted at this point. It has been said of old that this title originally derives from the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts).

Furthermore, although the texts of those two works overlap, their meanings are actually as different as heaven and earth. That [text] takes the "five assemblies" (*pañca-saṃgha*) as relying on the teachings to achieve observance;
"provisioning" (*zi*) refers to the sense of assisting in accomplishment. This meaning of "provisioning"—as in the relationship between teacher and student—is quite similar. Moreover...
The *Platform Sūtra* states: "Those of clear disposition all share this meaning. This differs from the current record, which takes "zi" (資) in the sense of assisting toward accomplishment.

Furthermore, the definitions and explanations of characters vary according to their usage; how could one claim that because the characters are the same, they must necessarily rely upon the preceding [text]?
Thus concludes the introduction regarding the purpose of establishing the title.

Furthermore, as interpretations from former times have differed, the *Zizhi* (Self-Support) established its title in profound accord with the Patriarch’s intent, encompassing both doctrine and practice, benefiting both self and others through its principles and meanings.
Because the traces of its refined influence were so vast, various commentaries and exegeses have emerged with mutual differences; some have been transmitted in writing, while others remain oral.

Now, taking those that are most prevalent, I shall briefly clarify three explanations: first, I will record their respective meanings, and subsequently, I will manifest the distinctions according to those meanings. It is not that there is anyone [who claims exclusive authority].

The commentary states: "The 'provision' (*zī*) belongs to the 'retention' (*bó*"; this refers to the text of the *ji* [commentary]. That is to say, as it says below regarding the classification and explanation of the words:

'retention' (*chí*) refers to the practice of the student. By extensively discerning the purport of the teaching within the text of the *ji*, it causes those students to give rise to practice based on the *ji*, thereby accomplishing the two types of retention.

If this is the case, the *ji* serves as the 'provision' (*néng-zī*). Furthermore, since the weighing and evaluating of matters and functions is also what the *ji* elucidates, how could it be otherwise?"
"Unable to support and maintain the practice" (my private note: this refers to Master Qin; now [the text] refutes Zhun). Furthermore, another explanation states:

the *Chao* (Excerpts) is titled by way of "practice" (*xing*), while the *Ji* (Record) is titled by way of "supporting and maintaining" (*zichi*), so that by means of the record one may penetrate the *chao*, thereby supporting and perfecting the intent of the three practices.

If one correlates these with the title of the *Chao*, then "supporting" (*zi*) corresponds to "practice" (*shi*), for it truly assists in manifesting the meaning of the practice and aids in clarifying its characteristics; as for "maintaining" (*chi*), it... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Regarding the three types of practice—practice through principle, practice through cause, and practice through action—which together constitute the two supports:

if one considers that which assists in manifesting ritual procedures (*śīlavidhi*) and illuminates the characteristics of the Vinaya (*vinayalakṣaṇa*) as the supported, then the *Shuochao* (Commentary on the Essentials) explaining these three practices is the supported, while the explanatory notes (*jishi*) clarifying the text of the *Shuochao* are the supporter.

Although it is said that the name is established based on the "matter" (*vastu*), the terms "ritual procedure" and "Vinaya characteristics" imply that both the supporter and the supported pertain to this category.

If one takes the meaning expounded in the extracted text as "practice," then since that is not a practice produced by the karmic activity of a learner (*śaikṣa*), how could it constitute the two types of upholding based on that?

Furthermore, another person explains: "The 'provisions' (*zī*) pertain to the teaching (*āgama*) which is the expressive medium, while the 'upholding' (*chí*) pertains to the practice (*pratipatti*) which is the expressed content;

because the teaching assists the practice, it is called 'Provisions and Upholding' (this is Master An’s interpretation in his *Preface and Explanation*). This interpretation relies on the explanatory text that follows."

Furthermore, if one were to cite the scriptural text and its commentary alone as "that which aids" (*zī*), it would not differ from the initial interpretation regarding what is to be refuted. The previous interpretation is concluded.
Third, the present correct meaning is set forth: "Aid" (*zī*) refers to the present record; "to employ" (*chí*) refers to the practice of the student; this is what the present record [addresses].

The "Explanation" (*vyākhyā*) does not merely distinguish the characteristics of the teaching; it provides a detailed exposition of its application and operation so that students may understand the teaching and clarify their practice, thereby supporting the accomplishment of the two types of upholding.
The subsequent section explains the words and phrases to distinguish the teaching, while weighing the functional utility to clarify practice.

Therefore, it is said that "teaching and practice are both propagated. Thus, one knows that the meaning of the teaching and the aspects of practice both belong to what is elucidated by the *Vyākhyā*, which supports the accomplishment of practice.

These two types of retention (*dhāraṇī*) are the functional efficacy of that [retention]. Furthermore, in the latter section, it is understood that the "expressive teaching"—namely names, phrases, and phonemes—is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), whereas the "signified meaning" is not subsumed under either of the two aggregates [form or consciousness]. Based on these two sections, the subject (the expressive) and the object (the signified) are distinct.

Question: In the introduction to the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the teaching and practice were first established; there, citing the commentary on the text, it states: "...teaching and practice... [and so forth].
Regarding the passage in the *Shuanghong* (Double Propagation) and other texts that further explains how the meaning of "teaching" (*jiao*) and "practice" (*xing*) is elucidated, it asks:

why does it cite the wording from the *Keshi* (Sectional Exegesis) alone to support the claim that the character "zi" (to assist/sustain) belongs to the teaching? Is this not a modification of the original commentary in the Preface? Answer:

In the section clarifying the ultimate meaning, [the author] merely refutes the attribution of the term "Zizhi" (Holding the Assistance) to the teaching as the signifier (*nengquan jiao*). Since it is actually that which assists [the practice], it is said to be cited alone. Therefore, what is being refuted here is the [erroneous] signification.
If the objects of cognition, their functions, and what is elucidated by the records can indeed assist those who practice and uphold [the teachings], then why would it not be so?

As for analyzing the text and correlating it with the practices taught in the scriptures, who does not know this? If that is the case, since they attribute the character "upholding" (*chi*) to "practice" (*xing*), I do not yet understand how this differs [from your position].
Answer: The movement of the mind toward an object and its active engagement constitute "practice. How could that which is expounded by the gates of the teachings itself be considered "practice"?

Question: The initial commentary states that "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*) refers to the practice of the learner itself, using the *Upadeśa* (Record) to extensively differentiate the characteristics of the teachings so that learners may give rise to practice through the Record and thereby accomplish the two types of upholding.

How does this differ from the current text, which further states that it causes learners to understand the teachings and clarify their practice, thereby supporting the accomplishment of the two types of upholding?
Answer: Although that [initial commentary] says that one accomplishes those two through the Record, [the meaning is essentially the same].
Master Chi [Zhiyi] takes the two types of upholding by the practitioner as the "practice" (*xing*) explained by the text; thus he says it is "teaching-practice" (*jiaoxing*).

Therefore, he states that the two types of upholding by the practitioner are the "practice" being explained. This is not the same as the present meaning, wherein both the signifier (*nengquan*) and the signified (*suquan*) belong to the category of "provision" (*zi*).

Rather, it is the practice of the practitioner’s two types of upholding that is "provisionally accomplished" (*zicheng*); thus one knows that the character *zi* (provision) refers to the present commentary.
This is the function [of the teaching]. Question: Furthermore, the practices (*caryā*) which are explained are intended to lead practitioners to cultivate those practices;

yet, the ultimate characteristics (*atyanta-lakṣaṇa*) now established are set forth vertically [as distinct]. Answer: The principles established here are fundamentally different. Based on the clarification of the capacity and the object of illumination, it is evident that the former is not the teaching that expresses;
rather, names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) are merely aggregates of matter (*rūpa-skandha*). As for the meanings and flavors (*artha-rasa*) expressed, they are...
Second, as for that which is not included: how can the practice that is the object of expression (*abhidheya*) itself be the person who trains (*śaikṣa*)?

Reflecting thus, I shall now explain the title of the *Commentary on the Practice of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya: Abridging the Excessive and Supplementing the Deficient*. This text is lofty and concise.

The meaning is profound and far-reaching; were it not for one who has accumulated learning to penetrate the subtle, exhaust the obscure, and fully realize the principles, how could one possibly attempt to deliberate upon it?

It is by the grace of our Master of the Record, the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master, who perfectly accords with the ancestral mind and meticulously investigates the purport of the teachings, that he wields his "celestial" pen like a cascading river of eloquence to compose this record, thereby enlightening those who are still ignorant. Whether establishing doctrines...
By means of annotations and appended texts, he elucidates the profound writings and abstruse meanings as clearly as pointing at the palm of one's hand.

Now, before explaining the *Shuochao* (Commentary on the Text), he first explains the preface to the *Ji* (Record). Thereupon, his disciple Vinaya Master An privately divided the text into topical sections and further composed an explanatory preface;
I shall now rely upon this. Searching for the topical headings, it says: *Sifenlü Xingshichao Zizhiji*, Volume One, Part One.

The first three characters of the title, "Bìngxù" (With Preface), designate the Vinaya as the primary authority followed, thereby distinguishing it from other schools; the subsequent three characters, "Suǒzōng" (What is Followed), designate the *Chāo* (Commentary) as the primary text followed, thereby distinguishing it from other writings.
These together constitute what is to be explained. The final three characters are the formal title of the present record (*jì*), which properly belongs to the explainer.

Regarding the titles of the Vinaya and the *Chāo*, the text itself will provide detailed clarification below. As for the title of this record, *Zīchí* (Supporting Maintenance), I shall now briefly examine the reasons for its establishment and the correspondence between its name and its reality.

The host of those who truly uphold [the teachings] names them after their masters; once the names are correctly established, they will not be deviant. This is precisely what Confucius meant when he said, "One must rectify names.

To explain this topic, it shall be divided into three sections. This compilation has been in circulation for barely six hundred years; from antiquity to the present, there have been sixty schools of exegesis.
At the head of each volume, names are inscribed, such as *Huizheng* (Compendium for Rectifying), *Xianzheng* (Manifesting Rectification), or *Jiyao* (Essential Collection).
To further illuminate the Garden of Meaning (*Arthavana*), I shall continue the lineage and supplement what was omitted; let each [work] maintain its integrity to manifest its distinctiveness.
I do not yet understand for what reason the author of the *Record* (*Juzhu*) sought to interpret various masters and established the title *Zizhi* (Self-Holding) as a distinct designation.

To trace its origins, the Vinaya as a teaching aims solely at the perfection of the study of precepts; it is fundamentally based on the protection of the senses against objects during both the initial reception and subsequent observance of the rules, such that one accords with them.

If one maintains [the precepts], it constitutes upholding; if one violates them, it constitutes an offense. Since the entire *Mahā-vinaya-piṭaka* explains nothing other than this, the commentary states:

"Although the texts that explain the teachings summarize and encompass [the rules], their primary purpose is solely to clarify upholding and violating. Although the text lists both upholding and violating, the underlying intent is to abandon violation and achieve upholding.
The Master of the Record (Jizang) deeply explored the fundamental source of the teachings and grasped the great outline of the *Vinaya-piṭaka*'s explanatory intent; therefore, he wrote thus.
To establish a virtuous name, if the name is not righteous, it will not be in accord with principle; how could one permit such arbitrary establishment?

One should know that this title, which reveals the entire intent of the section in a single stroke, is specifically the title of this *Śāstra*, and is in fact the title of the entire Great Canon (*Tripitaka*).

Since the Vinaya-piṭaka first flowed to this land, the five schools have vied in their expositions, yet the *Dharmaguptaka* school has been particularly propagated. Throughout the ages, [various masters...]
The Master [Daoxuan] either committed these to writing or transmitted them orally, extensively enumerating the chapters on doctrine (*yìzhāng*) for practical application (*xiàngxí*).

Yet, all were obscured by the texts, as illustrated by the following citation from the Preface to the *Jiàocháo*: "The records left behind by the various masters of previous generations consist merely of commentaries on the treatises and the establishment of questions and answers;
as for the essential *cháo* that manifests practical worldly affairs to serve as a model for future learners, there are none at all."
A *Yeshu* (Commentary on the Essentials) also states: "In recent times, there have been authors who have produced voluminous exegeses of the Vinaya texts;
yet while they can exhaustively expend their eloquence, they have not reached a definitive conclusion regarding actual practice.

For this reason, our Patriarch, manifesting his singular clarity and peerless wisdom, realized that the source of transformation lies solely in the performance of practice. Thus, he composed this work and titled it accordingly, so as to guide students."

This title expresses the intent to urge swift progress in cultivation, to protect the fundamental precepts received, to avoid transgressions and achieve observance, to alert the deluded toward the True, and to transform the ordinary into the Sage.

Therefore, the Master of the Record praised it, saying: "It alone sets aside all other teachers and transcends the nine generations [of patriarchs], fully embodying the Tathāgata’s skillful means and opening the gate of liberation for sentient beings; it is that by which the Three Jewels are sustained. (The fifth [section]).

The very purpose for which the *Cheng* (the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*) sets forth its course lies herein. Since antiquity, the chapters and records of the broad transmission have omitted this meaning;

thus, the *Jiaochao* (the *Fahua jing xuanyi jiaochao*) failed to reach it, focusing merely on verbal exegesis while entirely forgetting the practice of upholding [the precepts]. Therefore, our present school’s superior alignment with the Patriarch’s mind truly accords with the intent of the *Jiaochao*.

It was only fitting that the title of the *Zizhi* (the *Fahua jing xuanyi yishu zizhi chao*) was established, for as the text states: "The teaching arises according to the capacity of the recipient, and the upholding [of the precepts] proceeds from..."

The teaching reveals that the present "provisions" (*sambhāra*) belong to the expressive teaching (*vyañjana*), while the "support" (*dhāraṇa*) consists of the expressed practice (*artha*). Because the teaching assists practice, it is called "provision-support.

To cite the text as proof: "In analyzing and explaining the words and phrases, one values profound clarity regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and the weighing of their functional applications, so that one may effectively uphold the precepts in both their reception and subsequent observance.

Thus, when teaching and practice are both propagated, the benefit of oneself and others is simultaneously achieved. There are those who do not permit [the inclusion of] the teaching [within the provisions].

The establishment of the "Dual Practice" (*xiāngshùngxíng*) is based solely on the designation of "Single Practice" (*dānxíng*); thus, it is said that the two characters "Zīchí" (Supporting and Sustaining) both belong to practice.

This is not because there are three practices and two sustainings. If, in the preface, it says that the analysis and explanation of the text’s words deeply clarify the *dharmalakṣaṇa*, this is truly for the sake of accomplishing practice;
and even the meticulous observance of the precepts and their application is likewise only for the sake of accomplishing practice.

Now, it is said that while there is indeed a principle for [the *Sūtra*] to be practiced independently when it accords with the capacity of the practitioner, it would fail in establishing the framework of the teaching.

Therefore, regarding the title of this treatise, we must first interpret it according to the text as it stands so that the meaning of the passage has a clear point of reference. If it were practiced independently, it would belong to the category of "retention" (*dhāraṇī*).
However, I do not yet understand how the character *zī* (資) is to be paired; for *zī* means "to assist" or "to take up"—how could it be anything other than the teaching?
It should be understood that this statement briefly contains two faults. First, it contradicts the preface of the *Wenji* (Record of Explanations), which clearly states:

"The analysis and interpretation of the words values depth and clarity regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); is this not the Teaching (*śāsana*)? To weigh and evaluate practical applications so as to enable one to faithfully practice according to what has been received;

is this not Practice (*caryā*)? It then concludes by stating, "Teaching and Practice are both propagated. If one were to claim that this is merely the propagation of Practice alone, it would contradict this text.
Second, it would contradict both the meaning and the teaching. The teaching serves as the means of expression (*vācaka*), while practice is that which is expressed (*vācya*).

If there were no teaching, it would be difficult to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, and one could not discern the partial from the perfect. It is essential to receive the teaching and thereby open up understanding; only then can one establish practice based on that understanding.

When understanding and practice support one another, one may avoid all faults. If there were only practice without the teaching, it would be like walking without eyes—one would fail to recognize the path.

If one proceeds according to this [former] position, one will undoubtedly fall into error; one should know that the latter master establishes the title based on both teaching and practice, which accords with the Tathāgata’s intent for transformation and aligns with the spirit of the *Chaoji* (Commentary).
This overturns the two previous faults and achieves two gains and one success: first, it accords with the text; second, it accords with the meaning.
Furthermore, since this master was a preeminent disciple of Lingzhi, he must have personally heard the lectures and instructions. To a considerable extent...
Because one attains its true substance, it may be taken up. Generally, whenever the Buddhas and Patriarchs preach the Dharma, they do so in accordance with the capacities of beings;

thus, the teachings are necessarily formed by these capacities, and the capacities result in the formation of practice. Without capacity, there would be nothing for the teaching to apply; without teaching, there would be nothing for the capacity to point toward.

There has never been a teaching that does not accord with capacity, nor a capacity that does not receive the teaching. Now, the Master of the Record (Jizhu) has comprehensively recorded all that the Tathāgata has spoken within the Great Canon.

The Dharma teachings are established so that those who have left the household life in the final age may receive, practice, and uphold them; therefore, in setting forth the title, one must distinguish between teaching (*śāsana*) and practice (*pratipatti*).

This is because teaching is generally spoken of in relation to the capacities of sentient beings, whereas practice specifically belongs to the occasion when one receives the teaching according to those capacities.

Even if it were exclusively practice, how could it ever be divorced from the teaching? To say "teaching" does not necessarily imply practice, yet to speak of "practice" inherently includes the teaching. Such is the case.
This means that "provision" (*zī*) signifies assistance, while "retention" (*chí*) refers to the three practices; the practices refer to the two types of retention.

If one does not rely upon and receive the teachings of the *Vinaya* for guidance and the cultivation of wisdom and understanding, how can one recognize the characteristics of what is retained and what is transgressed?

Just as the distinction between beauty and ugliness cannot be known without a mirror, one must rely on the teachings before being able to establish one's practice. Thus, the single character "provision" (*zī*) certainly belongs to this category.
That the single word "upholding" (*chí*) necessarily pertains to practice is beyond doubt. As the preface to the record states:

"In categorizing and explaining words and phrases, it is vital to have a profound understanding of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics)"—this pair of lines clarifies that the teaching defines and measures the application of things;

and "so as to enable one to strictly observe the precepts in both their reception and subsequent practice"—this pair of lines clarifies practice. Thus, when teaching and practice are propagated together, the benefit of both self and others is achieved. These two [points]...
The two lines of the double conclusion summarize the titles at the beginning of the teaching and practice; these two lines precisely manifest that the titles encompass both teaching and practice.
Since the preceding text has already explained teaching and practice individually, and the subsequent text explains teaching and practice collectively, it then returns to the titles;
thus, this constitutes a general discussion of teaching and practice. The following text, moreover, represents the general within the particular and the particular within the general.
Because the meanings of the distinct characteristics converge upon a single principle, the title at the beginning of the work fully reveals the intent of the entire section.
Since the teaching and practice are fully revealed, if the title were considered merely in terms of practice alone, it would be erroneous to claim that the intent of the section is fully revealed;

the clear evidence for this is found here, as explained in the commentary on the preface to the *Shu-chao*, which states: "The first preface is divided into three major sections; the first clarifies the authorship..."
The "Shu" (Exposition) merely narrates the teachings that express [the meaning]; it sets forth ten gates to encompass the significance of all chapters.

Both the text and its meaning belong to the teaching (*śāsana*), yet the teaching is not in vain, for its ultimate aim is to guide practice. Therefore, the latter part is divided into three sections on practice to subsume the various capacities of sentient beings.

Thus, the beginning and end of both teaching and practice are complete. (Text) The *Chao* (Commentary) clearly demonstrates teaching and practice; the Master of the Record relies upon the text therein.

How could Master Shi have established the title as referring exclusively to "practice" (xing)? By briefly citing two passages as evidence, we know that Zashi’s establishment of the title indicates that the teaching and practice are mutually integrated.
